birthplace: Buckingham Square, Cork, Ireland, born on 15 January 1798, the only son of Major Thomas Croker; he was bound apprentice to merchants in Cork and Lisbon before removing to London, where his official and literary life was passed
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the antiquarian folk-collecting strand of Irish Romanticism, which gathered fairy legends, keens and popular song from the south of Ireland and set them beside the metrical romance and the national tale; an Irish writer working in the London book and periodical trade
literary_identity: Antiquary and folklorist, collector and editor of Irish fairy legends, songs and traditions; the first substantial English-language collector of southern Irish folk narrative, and a London clerk of letters
biography: Thomas Crofton Croker was born in Cork on 15 January 1798, the only son of Major Thomas Croker, and was apprenticed to merchants in Cork and Lisbon before settling in London, where from about 1818 until his retirement in February 1850 he was a clerk in the Admiralty, augmenting a modest salary with literary work and serving from 1837 as registrar of the Royal Literary Fund. His rambles through the south of Ireland between 1812 and 1816 had yielded folk songs, keens and fairy traditions, and a collection of orally transmitted poems brought him in 1818 into touch with Thomas Moore. Researches in the South of Ireland (1824) laid this spoil before the public, and the Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland, beginning in 1825 with later series to 1828, made his name; it went out with no author's name on the title page, because Croker had lost his originals and let passages be rewritten by friends, among them William Maginn. Legends of the Lakes, or Sayings and Doings at Killarney (1829), illustrated by William Maclise, followed, and The Popular Songs of Ireland (1839) gathered his life's collecting. On 30 March 1830 he married at Barnes, Surrey, Marianne Nicholson, only daughter of the watercolour painter Francis Nicholson (1792-1854); their only son, Thomas Francis Dillon Croker, born 26 August 1831, became an antiquary and edited his father's papers. Croker died at Old Brompton, London, on 8 August 1854, and his wife survived him only a short time.
literary_profile: His books are collections rather than compositions, and their art is that of the frame, the selection and the note. Researches in the South of Ireland (1824) mixes topographical narrative, legend and translated verse from the southern counties; the Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland (series of the later 1820s, reissued in new editions with illustrations, one of them dated 1844) gathers the fairy and ghost tale of Cork and Kerry, its best-known piece the Legend of O'Donoghue of the Killarney lakes, and its later arrangements class the Irish folk beings as sheerie, cluricaune, banshee, phouka, merrow, dullahan and fir darrig; Legends of the Lakes, or Sayings and Doings at Killarney (1829) applies the same method to lake legend with Maclise's designs; and The Popular Songs of Ireland (1839), with its companion treatment of the keen, prints the airs and verses he had transcribed since 1812. The Dictionary of National Biography also lists an early piece called 'The Talisman' (1820) among his works, and his son reported that other books, among them 'The Adventures of Barney Mahoney', belonged to other hands.
stylistic_characteristics: His prose is that of the conversational antiquary: brisk, garrulous and first-person, framing each tale as something heard from a named narrator at a named place, then annotating it with parallels from other European collections. The retellings are deliberately comic and vernacular, softening what the tradition gives bluntly, and that humour is the ground on which Yeats afterwards reproached him for sentimentalising Irish tale-telling. Scholarship travels in the notes and appended songs rather than in argument, and he prints the keens and laments as seriously as the fairy romance. His manner belongs to the Scottish popular-antiquarian vogue of the post-Waverley decade and to the song-editing practice of Moore's Irish Melodies, both of which he knew at first hand.
intellectual_concerns: Whether Ireland possessed a vernacular mythology worth recovering before it disappeared under the pressures of the 1820s and the famine years that followed; the relation of Irish folk narrative to the German, Scandinavian and Celtic corpora, with which his work was compared and into whose circulation it passed; the evidential value of legend, place-name and song for history and topography; the authenticity of a retelling, made a live question by his own unsigned and collaboratively rewritten title pages; and the antiquary's civic loyalties, where official record work, patronage and the Royal Literary Fund meet.
historical_significance: He created the first permanent repertory of Irish folk narrative in English, and the Fairy Legends made that repertory part of European Romantic folklore: the book was praised by Sir Walter Scott, was translated into German in the later 1820s and entered the orbit of the Brothers Grimm, whose own influence on Irish collecting his case exemplifies. His songs, keens and legends were a storehouse for writers of the Irish literary revival, which used them even while W. B. Yeats blamed him for humourising the tales; his son's editions and the learned societies he joined kept his record work in use. As an instance of the anonymous, collaborative and partly rewoven condition of early folk collecting, his texts are now standard evidence in the history of folklore studies.
biographical_uncertainty: The dating of the Fairy Legends is unsettled - the Dictionary of National Biography gives 1825, 1827 and 1834 for the successive issues while modern accounts speak of three series from 1825 to 1828, and the year of the German translation is given as 1826 by the Dictionary of Irish Biography and variously elsewhere. Authorship is disputed at several points: the first series went out anonymously because Croker had lost his manuscripts and let Maginn and other friends rewrite parts; 'The Adventures of Barney Mahoney' is dated 1832 by Ricorso and 1852 by the Dictionary of National Biography, and Ricorso and his son's testimony would give it to his wife Marianne Nicholson Croker; and 'The Talisman' (1820) rests on the Dictionary of National Biography alone. His mother's name and fortunes, and the share in his collections of Richard Sainthill and of the manuscripts of R. Adolphus Lynch, are variously reported. No influence relationship could be verified strongly enough to record, so major_influences is left empty: Scott's praise and Moore's acquaintance are relations of reception and friendship, not documented influence.

birthplace: Sussex County, Delaware, born in 1795, the day and month unknown, of free parents; he was educated and trained for the ministry in the African Presbyterian connection of Philadelphia and New York, and spent his working life in New York City
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the African-American free-Black press and pulpit literature of the early republic, spanning Freedom's Journal and the New York coloured newspapers of the 1820s to the 1850s, and the transatlantic controversy over colonisation and emancipation
literary_identity: Presbyterian minister, printer and editor; co-founder and first editor of Freedom's Journal (1827), the first newspaper in the United States owned and edited by African Americans
biography: Samuel Eli Cornish was born in 1795 in Sussex County, Delaware, of free parents, and grew up to be one of the most influential African-American men of letters in New York before 1860. The Presbytery of Philadelphia launched his ministry in 1819 and he was ordained in 1822, afterwards preaching in New York City and gathering the first African Presbyterian church there, whose pastorate he held for years. In March 1827 he and John Brown Russwurm, a Bowdoin College graduate then teaching school in Boston, founded Freedom's Journal in New York, recognised by the Library of Congress as the first African-American-owned and -edited newspaper in the United States; it began weekly publication on 16 March 1827 and Cornish served as its senior editor. He withdrew in September 1827 over the colonisation question, which he opposed while his colleague came to advocate removal to Africa, and the paper, in its last months under Russwurm alone, endorsed the colonisation societies before ceasing publication in 1829. Cornish answered with The Rights of All, launched in the spring of 1829, which lived less than a year, and from 1837 to 1839 he edited with Philip A. Bell and Charles B. Ray the Colored American, which had begun as the Weekly Advocate in January 1837 and took its known name on 4 March 1837. He continued to preach, to publish and to plead for the moral, educational and economic betterment of the coloured people of New York until his death at Brooklyn on 6 November 1858; he had married Jane Livingston and left children.
literary_profile: His surviving writing is occasional and editorial rather than bookish. The numbers of Freedom's Journal (16 March 1827 onward) carry his opening claim that the people of colour must be able to speak for themselves and no longer need anyone to define them, together with editorials on slavery and the slave trade, on the pretensions of the colonisation societies, on education, temperance and industry, and letters, statistics and notices of African-American churches, schools and achievements drawn from the Black communities of the Atlantic states. The Rights of All (1829-30) was his own weekly reply to Russwurm's emigrationism, and the Colored American (1837-9) gave him a larger organ for the same programme of self-help, denominational news and antislavery argument; his name also appears as a contributor to that paper's numbers after his editorial connection ended, and a speech or address of his is recorded in the abolitionist archive for October 1839. No independent volume of sermons or treatises by him survives in the accounts consulted here.
stylistic_characteristics: His manner is that of the coloured pulpit turned to editorial use: earnest, declarative, and built on the first-person plural, with the balanced period of the moral essay and the cadence of scripture. The argument is usually from conceded premises to a demand for recognition rather than from statistical detail, and the tone shifts between remonstrance with white patronage, exhortation to his own community, and irony at the colonisation societies. Self-representation is his governing device: the paper's independence is itself the claim, and his editorials treat the act of printing as evidence of capacity.
intellectual_concerns: The right and duty of the oppressed to speak in their own voice in print; the moral and economic elevation of the free Black population through churches, schools, temperance and skilled labour; the colonisation controversy and the claim that removal to Africa could solve the problem of American slavery and prejudice; the relation between the abolitionist cause and white benevolent societies; citizenship, nativity and belonging in a republic that denied both; and the education and self-government of the coloured ministry.
historical_significance: As first editor of Freedom's Journal he broke the white monopoly on the public representation of African Americans and founded the Black press tradition that ran through the Colored American and the later abolitionist newspapers; his resignation of 1827 and the success of The Rights of All mark the opening of the quarrel between abolitionist immediatism and colonisation emigrationism, a division that shaped Black politics for two decades. The New York coloured Presbyterian church he gathered is a landmark in African-American religious history, and his career is the standard case in histories of the Black press of the minister-editor who makes a newspaper an instrument of communal self-definition.
biographical_uncertainty: Only the year of his birth is settled, and it is given as 1795 with the day and month unknown, some genealogical and encyclopedic accounts printing 'about 1795' or '1795?'; his birth in Sussex County, Delaware, rests on the account of his life in the BlackPast and New-York Historical Society sketches. The date at which he founded or took the pastorate of the first African Presbyterian church in New York is variously given as 1821, 1822 and 1829, and the order of his licences and settlements cannot be established from the sources consulted. The opening of The Rights of All is dated April 1829 by some accounts and May 1829 by others, and its end is reported as 'less than a year' and as 1829-30. His editorial connection with the Colored American is given as 1837-9 while the paper ran to 1842. His death is usually given as 6 November 1858 at Brooklyn, but another modern account places it in August 1858. No influence relationship could be verified strongly enough to record, so major_influences is left empty.

birthplace: Port Antonio, Jamaica, then a British slaveholding colony, born on 1 October 1799 (some accounts give 1 May), the son of a white English father and an enslaved Black mother; he was sent to school in Quebec and in 1812 removed to Maine, where he attended the Hebron Academy
nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American, Jamaican-born; the free-Black print culture of the early American republic and the emigrationist and colonisation writing it produced, passing into the literature of the Liberia settlements
literary_identity: Journalist, teacher and public officer; co-founder and after 1827 sole editor of Freedom's Journal, afterwards editor of the Liberia Herald and governor of the Maryland colony in Africa
biography: John Brown Russwurm was born at Port Antonio in Jamaica on 1 October 1799, the son of an English father and a woman held in slavery, and was educated at a school in Quebec before passing to Maine in 1812 with his father, where he worked his way through the Hebron Academy. He entered Bowdoin College, graduated in 1826 as the first African American to take a degree there and, as the college itself records, is thought to be the third African American to graduate from an American college; he was elected to Phi Beta Kappa in September 1826. He taught at a school for African-American children in Boston, and in March 1827 he and the Reverend Samuel E. Cornish established Freedom's Journal in New York, the first African-American-owned newspaper in the United States, whose first number appeared on 16 March 1827. Cornish withdrew in September 1827 and Russwurm conducted the paper alone to its last number in 1829, during its final months openly advocating African colonisation, the position that divided him from his colleague and from the emerging immediatist abolitionists. In November 1829 he emigrated to Liberia, where he edited the Liberia Herald from 1830, served the colony as secretary and as agent of the Maryland State Colonization Society, took charge of its schools and education work, and from 1836 was governor of the Maryland colony in Africa, a post he held until his death at Harper on 9 June 1851. He married Sarah McGill and left children; his life and writings were edited and republished by Winston James as those of a pan-Africanist pioneer.
literary_profile: His writing divides into two careers. In New York and Boston it is the journalism of Freedom's Journal (1827-29): editorials on slavery and the slave trade, on the claims and capacities of the coloured people, addresses to African-American societies and churches, and the arguments for African emigration with which he brought the paper to a close; these numbers are the earliest substantial body of opinion printed by an African-American college graduate. In Liberia his work is that of a colonial editor and official - the numbers of the Liberia Herald from 1830, official reports and addresses of the Maryland colony, tracts and letters on the settlement's agriculture, schools and relations with the United States and with the American Colonization Society, and the case for the colony's absorption into Liberia which occupied him through the 1840s. Nothing of his Bowdoin exercise writing or of his Boston teaching survives in the accounts consulted here as a separate literary work.
stylistic_characteristics: His prose is that of a classically trained rhetorician of the college exercise school: formal, periodic and heavily subordinate, with a moralist's apparatus of example and appeal to providential history. The Freedom's Journal editorials are argumentative and conciliatory at once, addressed to white as well as Black readers, and their diction is far nearer the Augustan essay than to the prophetic manner of the later abolitionist press; his letters as a colonisation official are administrative, evidential and self-justifying, pressed into the defence of an unpopular policy. Where Cornish writes as the pastor exhorting his flock, Russwurm writes as the editor-convinced of a scheme, and his later prose is increasingly that of the report and the minute.
intellectual_concerns: Whether the people of colour could hope for citizenship in the United States, and therefore whether separate national life in Africa was the prudent or the necessary course; the education and moral elevation of African Americans as the proof of capacity; the ownership and control of Black representation in print, which he shared with Cornish in founding the first Black newspaper; the character, government, agriculture and commerce of the Liberia settlements; the responsibility of the slaveholding colonies, Jamaica including, and the Atlantic world of plantation slavery out of which he came; and the relation of race, Christianity and civilisation in the missionary and colonisation literature of the 1830s and 1840s.
historical_significance: He was the first African American to graduate from an American college to enter journalism, and as co-founder and then sole editor of Freedom's Journal he helped create the Black press; as a Jamaican-born, US-educated emigrant he became the most prominent individual convert to organised colonisation, and his governorship of the Maryland colony made him the leading African-American public figure in Liberia, a standing which the American Colonization Society used in its propaganda and which the abolitionist press, from Freedom's Journal's successor papers onward, treated as a defection. Modern scholarship, helped by Winston James's collection of his life and writings, reads him as a pan-Africanist pioneer rather than a renegade, and his career is the central case study of the colonisation split in early Black American politics.
biographical_uncertainty: His birth date is given as 1 October 1799 by the Smithsonian portrait record and the usual modern accounts, with 1 May 1799 reported elsewhere, and his birth at Port Antonio rests on those modern accounts; his mother's name is not recorded in the sources consulted here, and his father's identity and standing are variously described. The end of Freedom's Journal is variously placed in February, March or December 1829, and his sole editorship is accordingly dated by different authorities. His Liberian offices are unevenly reported: modern accounts give him as editor of the Liberia Herald from 1830, as colonial secretary, as agent of the colonization society in the United States and as governor of the Maryland colony from 1836, but the exact sequence and the dates of the secretarial and agency years differ, and the founding of a school or institute at Cape Palmas attributed to him could not be verified here. His place of death is given as Harper and as Cape Palmas, and the number of his children as four or six. No influence relationship could be verified strongly enough to record, so major_influences is left empty.
